scenes.onScreen: "Default arguments and overloading": numbered lines (1. A default value fills a missing argument; 2. Overloads share a name but differ in parameters; 3. The compiler picks the best match) and an analogy card: a tea stall: the usual order is chai, but you can ask for coffee
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A default argument is a value that the compiler uses when the caller leaves it out. Overloading means several functions share one name, but have different parameters. The compiler picks the one that matches the call best. Think of a tea stall. The usual order is chai, but you may ask for coffee.

scenes.onScreen: power.cpp: power has a default exponent of two
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] The parameter exp has a default of two. [HL 6] The loop multiplies the base, exp times. [HL 13] The call power of five leaves out exp. The default of two is used. The answer is twenty-five. [HL 14] The call power of two and ten gives one thousand and twenty-four.

scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: Look at the three calls. The compiler checks the number of arguments, and their types. One int picks the first function. Two ints pick the second. One double picks the third.

diagram.caption: a table of calls and the functions that the compiler picks

scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] Area of one int is a square. [HL 5] Area of two ints is a rectangle. [HL 6] Area of a double is a circle. [HL 9] Five is an int, so we get twenty-five. [HL 10] Four and six give twenty-four. [HL 11] Two point zero is a double, so we get twelve point five six.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as overload dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints twenty-five, twenty-four and twelve point five six.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A default argument fills in a missing value. Two. Defaults go at the end of the parameter list. Three. Overloads share a name but have different parameters. Four. The compiler picks the best match. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: An ambiguous call
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We call show with the plain number five. There is a long version and a double version. The compiler says the call is ambiguous. An int fits both equally well. Write five with the letter L, or add an int version.

scenes.onScreen: I overloaded my function. Now it has a lot on its plate, but it keeps its name.

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

show.cpp: In function 'int main()':
show.cpp:8:9: error: call of overloaded 'show(int)' is ambiguous
    8 |     show(5);
      |     ~~~~^~~
show.cpp:4:6: note: candidate: 'void show(long int)'
    4 | void show(long n) { cout << "long " << n << endl; }
bug.why: An int converts to long and to double with the same cost, so the compiler cannot choose. Make the type exact, or add an int overload.

pun: "I overloaded my function. Now it has a lot on its plate, but it keeps its name."
challenge: Write two functions called describe. One takes an int and one takes a string. Call both.
challengeAnswer: Write void describe with an int parameter and void describe with a string parameter. Call describe with seven and with a quoted word.
